title: Perimeter & Area
coreInsight: Perimeter measures boundary length while area measures two-dimensional coverage, and area formulas arise from composing or rearranging simpler regions.
targetLearnerRealization: Perimeter counts linear units around a boundary while area counts square units covering an interior; fixing one does not fix the other.
learningObjectives: Distinguish boundary length from interior coverage.
Derive rectangle area from rows of unit squares.
Use linear units for perimeter and square units for area.
Recognize that equal perimeter need not imply equal area and equal area need not imply equal perimeter.
Use a perpendicular height in triangle area even when it is not a visible side.

continuity.openingCallback: Treat one unit square as a whole region and distinguish its covered fraction from the one-dimensional lengths around it.
closingSeeds: An irregular region can be cut or completed into familiar shapes.
A circle needs new ways to measure its curved boundary and interior.

misconceptionTargets.misconception: Area and perimeter formulas can be swapped.
The height in an area formula must be a visible side of the shape.
Square units are optional notation rather than part of the quantity.

beats.purpose: Force a choice between measuring the boundary and measuring the covered interior.
beats.expectedRealization: The same rectangle has two different quantities with different units.
beats.transitionIn: Fractions named how much of a whole region was selected. Now separate the region from the path around it.
beats.whyNow: A concrete floor-and-trim context exposes formula swapping before any formula is given.
beats.entryBridge: Decide whether each material travels around the edge or fills the inside.
beats.exitBridge: Trim uses 14 linear meters; tiles cover 12 square meters.
learnerPrompts: Which measurement buys trim, and which buys floor tiles?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. The boundary is 14 m; the covered interior is 12 m².
beats.incorrectFeedback: Trace the trim around all four sides, then count the one-meter squares that cover the floor.

visual.ariaLabel: Fourteen linear boundary units contrasted with twelve square interior units for a four by three rectangle

steps.title: Trace the edge
steps.body: A 4 m by 3 m rectangle has boundary 4 + 3 + 4 + 3 = 14 m.

steps.title: Tile the inside
steps.body: Three rows of four unit squares cover 3 × 4 = 12 m².

resolution.takeaway: Perimeter measures around; area measures inside.

beats.purpose: Derive rectangle area as an array of unit squares and secure square units.
beats.expectedRealization: Length times width counts rows times squares per row.
beats.transitionIn: Keep the 4-by-3 interior and count its tiles by structure instead of one at a time.
beats.prompt: A rectangle holds 5 rows of 8 unit squares. What is its area?
beats.correctFeedback: Yes. Five rows of eight squares cover 40 square units.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Area counts every unit square: multiply rows by squares per row and keep square units.

steps.title: Count the array
steps.body: 5 × 8 = 40 unit squares. This array count is why rectangle area is length × width.

resolution.takeaway: Rectangle area multiplies two lengths to count square units.

beats.purpose: Show that fixed area does not fix perimeter.
beats.expectedRealization: Rearranging the same number of unit squares changes exposed boundary length.
beats.transitionIn: Forty tiles can form different rectangles. Try a smaller set whose edges are easy to trace.
beats.prompt: A 3-by-4 rectangle and a 2-by-6 rectangle each use 12 unit squares. Which statement is true?

options.text: They have equal area, but perimeters 14 and 16.
They have equal area and equal perimeter.
They have different area, but equal perimeter.
They have different area and different perimeter.

beats.correctFeedback: Correct. Coverage is fixed at 12 squares while the exposed edge changes.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Compute coverage and boundary separately for each rectangle.

visual.ariaLabel: Two rectangles with equal area twelve and different perimeters fourteen and sixteen

resolution.takeaway: Equal area does not force equal perimeter.

beats.purpose: Derive triangle area by pairing copies and detach height from slanted side length.
beats.expectedRealization: Two matching triangles form a parallelogram, so one triangle has half of base times perpendicular height.
beats.transitionIn: A rectangle's rows stand perpendicular to its base. Slide the top row sideways: the slanted side changes, but the vertical row count does not.
beats.prompt: A triangle has base 10 cm and perpendicular height 6 cm. A slanted side is 8 cm. What is its area?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. Half of 10 × 6 is 30 cm²; the 8 cm side is not the perpendicular height.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Pair two copies into a base-10, height-6 parallelogram, then take half.

steps.title: Double the triangle
steps.body: Two matching copies form a parallelogram with area 10 × 6 = 60 cm².

steps.title: Take one copy
steps.body: One triangle has area 60 ÷ 2 = 30 cm². Height is the perpendicular separation from base to opposite vertex.

resolution.takeaway: Triangle area is one half of base times perpendicular height.

beats.purpose: Name the measurements and formulas after their unit structures have been built.
beats.expectedRealization: The formulas encode tracing or tiling operations rather than interchangeable symbol patterns.
beats.name: Perimeter and area
beats.conciseDefinition: Perimeter is total boundary length in linear units. Area is interior coverage in square units. Rectangle area counts a unit-square array; triangle area is half a base-height parallelogram.
beats.formalization: rectangle P = 2l + 2w · rectangle A = lw · triangle A = bh/2
beats.memoryHook: Trace for perimeter; tile for area; height meets base at 90°.

beats.purpose: Destroy the fixed-perimeter/fixed-area misconception with an authentic reshape.
beats.expectedRealization: The same 120-foot boundary encloses 500 square feet as a 50-by-10 rectangle and 900 as a 30-by-30 square.
beats.transitionIn: Twelve tiles kept area while the edge changed. Reverse the experiment: lock the edge and reshape the interior.
beats.whyNow: The learner can independently track boundary and coverage, so the fence constraint becomes a meaningful contrast rather than a formula exercise.
beats.entryBridge: Compute the fence once, redistribute it into four equal sides, then compare covered areas.
beats.exitBridge: Boundary stays 120 feet while coverage rises by 400 square feet.
beats.reusedRepresentation: A fixed-length boundary surrounding changing rows of unit squares.
learnerPrompts: What is the original rectangle's area?
How many feet of fence stay fixed?
What square side uses that same fence?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. The square gains 900 − 500 = 400 square feet.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Keep perimeter and area in separate lines: find the 120-foot fence, then the square side, then compare areas.

steps.title: Redistribute the fence
steps.body: A square splits 120 feet into four equal sides, so each side is 30 feet.

steps.title: Compare coverage
steps.body: The square covers 30 × 30 = 900 ft², an increase of 900 − 500 = 400 ft².

resolution.takeaway: A fixed boundary can enclose different areas; keep the two quantities and their units distinct.

beats.purpose: Assess perimeter and area together without formula swapping.
beats.whyNow: Return to a simple rectangle after the reshape.
beats.entryBridge: Write one boundary calculation and one coverage calculation.
beats.exitBridge: The results are 30 cm and 44 cm².
learnerPrompts: Which answer needs linear units and which needs square units?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. Perimeter is 30 cm and area is 44 cm².
beats.incorrectFeedback: Add all four sides for perimeter; multiply the two dimensions for area.

resolution.takeaway: Compute and label boundary and coverage separately.

beats.purpose: Assess the dimensional meaning of square units.
beats.whyNow: Make the unit distinction the target rather than a decoration.
beats.entryBridge: Ask what one counted unit looks like.
learnerPrompts: Is the measurement counting segments, squares, or cubes?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. Carpet coverage is measured in square yards.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Carpet covers a two-dimensional surface, so each unit is a unit square.

steps.body: A 7-yard by 5-yard carpet covers 35 one-yard squares, so its area is 35 yd².

resolution.takeaway: Units record the dimension of what was counted.

beats.whyNow: Repeat the garden structure with smaller values and no animation support.
beats.entryBridge: Verify the perimeter equality before comparing products.
beats.exitBridge: Both perimeters are 20, but the 5-by-5 square has area 25 versus 16.
learnerPrompts: What remains fixed, and which product changes?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. The square encloses 9 more square units.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Compute each perimeter and each area on separate lines.

steps.body: The 2-by-8 rectangle has P = 20 and A = 16. The 5-by-5 square has P = 20 and A = 25, so the gain is 9.

resolution.takeaway: Equal perimeter does not imply equal area.

beats.purpose: Assess selection of perpendicular height over a visible slanted side.
beats.whyNow: Change the geometry while keeping the base-height model.
beats.entryBridge: Locate the segment perpendicular to the chosen base.
learnerPrompts: Which given length meets the base at 90°?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. The area is 30 square units.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Use the perpendicular height 5, not the slanted side 7.

resolution.takeaway: Height is perpendicular distance, not necessarily a side.

beats.purpose: Assess constructing another rectangle of equal area and comparing boundaries.
beats.whyNow: Finish by coordinating factor pairs with geometric meaning.
beats.entryBridge: Preserve the product, then compare sums of side lengths.
beats.exitBridge: Both areas are 36, while perimeters are 26 and 24.
learnerPrompts: Which factor pair preserves 36 square units, and what happens to its doubled sum?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. A 4-by-9 rectangle has the same area and a 26-unit perimeter.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Find a factor pair of 36, then compute its perimeter independently.

steps.body: 4 × 9 = 36, matching the 6-by-6 area. Its perimeter is 2(4 + 9) = 26, compared with 24 for the square.

resolution.takeaway: Factor pairs can preserve coverage while changing boundary.

beats.purpose: Consolidate meaning, units, formulas, and height choice.
beats.expectedRealization: The measured object determines the operation and unit.
beats.transitionIn: Floors, trim, tiles, fences, rectangles, and triangles all demanded a decision about what was being measured before any arithmetic.
beats.prompt: Which actions belong in a reliable perimeter-and-area routine? Select all four.

options.text: Decide whether the target is boundary or coverage.
Connect the formula to tracing, tiling, or rearranging.
For triangle area, use perpendicular height to the chosen base.
Use linear units for perimeter and square units for area.

response.feedback: Each action keeps the measurement meaningful.

beats.correctFeedback: Yes. Identify the object, justify the model, choose true height, and carry the right units.
beats.incorrectFeedback: All four protect against swapping formulas or dimensions.

steps.body: The formula is the last step of a measurement decision: trace an edge, count unit squares, or halve a paired base-height region.

resolution.takeaway: Meaning first, formula second, units always.

beats.purpose: Create the need for area decomposition.
beats.expectedRealization: A shape without a single familiar formula can still be measured by cutting or completing it.
beats.transitionIn: Rectangles tile directly, and a triangle becomes half a paired region. Now remove the convenient outer shape.
beats.prompt: An L-shaped floor has no single formula on our list. How could rectangles still reveal its area without counting every square one by one?
beats.takeaway: A difficult region may become simple after a useful cut, subtraction, or rearrangement.

notes: Design: trim versus floor tiles distinguishes boundary from coverage before formulas. Unit-square arrays derive rectangle area, equal-area rectangles separate area from perimeter, and paired triangles derive the perpendicular base-height formula. The authentic garden reverses the comparison by fixing perimeter and changing area.

Beat outline: boundary-or-cover anchor -> tile arrays -> same area/different edge -> triangle height -> name measurements -> authentic fixed-fence contrast -> five independent problems -> consolidation -> irregular-region hook.

The mapped garden animation is referenced unchanged after submission across its five declared states. Existing bars-and-groups and choice-grid visuals suffice; no renderer or animation source changes were made.

Generated results were recomputed by boundary sums, unit-square products, and base-height area, with independent factor-pair, dimensional-unit, or alternative-theorem audits. The lesson remains draft pending human review.
